subject: Copywriting
title: John E. Powers: The Honest Copywriter
description: A quick win: understand John E. Powers: The Honest Copywriter.

hook.text: In 1880, John E. Powers wrote: 'We have a lot of rotten umbrellas that we want to get rid of.' The store sold out.

buildup.text: Powers is considered the first modern copywriter. He worked for Wanamaker's, the first department store.

discovery.text: His approach was radical honesty. He described products truthfully, including their flaws. Customers trusted him.

twist.text: Wanamaker fired Powers for being too honest. But sales dropped so much they hired him back at double the salary.

climax.text: Powers proved that honesty sells better than hype. His direct style influenced every copywriter who came after.

punchline.text: Rotten umbrellas sold out. Honesty is powerful copy.

quiz.question: Why was John E. Powers fired and then rehired?
options: Too honest, but sales dropped without him

details.summary: John E. Powers is widely considered the first professional copywriter in history. Working in the 1880s, he revolutionized advertising by insisting on honest, straightforward prose when the industry relied on exaggeration and hype. His style was so effective that stores saw sales double on days...
details.whyItMatters: Powers proved that honesty could be the most persuasive sales technique. His legacy challenges the assumption that great copy must be manipulative.
takeaways: Powers is regarded as the world's first professional copywriter
He insisted on plain truth in an era of exaggerated advertising claims
Stores reported sales doubling on days his advertisements appeared

faq.question: Why was John E. Powers considered revolutionary?
faq.answer: In the 1880s, ads were full of wild claims and circus-style hype. Powers wrote simple, honest statements like 'We have a lot of rotten gossamers we want to get rid of.' His candor shocked the industry but built tremendous consumer trust.

faq.question: Did Powers's honest approach actually sell products?
faq.answer: Yes — dramatically. John Wanamaker's department store saw sales double on days Powers's ads ran. His honesty created trust, and trust created loyal customers. He proved that respecting the reader's intelligence was the most effective long-term strategy.
